Using Copilot (Basic) to analyse the data

Initial prompt

Write the code to analyse the data in the attcheched csv file in R. I am wanting to predict the number of recruit at a plot (recruits) related to the percentage of soil crust at that site (crust). The file is called df_rec_saw.csv and is located in the folder data relative to the workspace.

Looking at df_rec_saw, the response variable is a count (recruits) with many zeros and some very large values (up to >100), so I would start with a negative binomial GLM and then assess whether there is evidence for excess zeros.

Fit models

Fit both a Poisson and negative binomial model and compare them.

# Poisson GLM
m_pois <- glm(
  recruits ~ crust,
  family = poisson,
  data = df
)

# Negative binomial GLM
m_nb <- glm.nb(
  recruits ~ crust,
  data = df
)

summary(m_pois)

Check overdispersion

check_overdispersion(m_pois)
# Overdispersion test

       dispersion ratio =    43.409
  Pearson's Chi-Squared = 13803.924

Overdispersion detected.
check_overdispersion(m_nb)
# Overdispersion test

 dispersion ratio = 0.976
          p-value = 0.896
No overdispersion detected.

A dispersion ratio >> 1 for the Poisson model would indicate overdispersion and support using the negative binomial.

Model diagnostics

sim_nb <- simulateResiduals(m_nb)

plot(sim_nb)
testDispersion(sim_nb)

    DHARMa nonparametric dispersion test via sd of residuals fitted vs.
    simulated

data:  simulationOutput
dispersion = 0.97584, p-value = 0.896
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
testZeroInflation(sim_nb)

    DHARMa zero-inflation test via comparison to expected zeros with
    simulation under H0 = fitted model

data:  simulationOutput
ratioObsSim = 1.0093, p-value = 0.944
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
testUniformity(sim_nb)

    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  simulationOutput$scaledResiduals
D = 0.035836, p-value = 0.8057
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

The zero-inflation test will indicate whether you need a zero-inflated model.

The exponentiated coefficient gives the multiplicative change in expected recruits for a one-unit increase in crust.

Because crust ranges from 0 to ~0.9, it is often easier to interpret a 10% increase:

beta <- coef(m_nb)["crust"]

exp(beta * 0.1)
    crust 
0.9012501

Cook’s distance

Given the very large counts in some plots, I would also examine influential observations.

cook <- cooks.distance(m_nb)

plot(cook,

abline(

  col = "red",
  lty = 2
)

  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low,

  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = df,
             aes(crust, recruits),
             inherit.aes = FALSE,
             alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_bw()

Given the structure of this dataset, my expectation is that the negative binomial model will strongly outperform Poisson due to overdispersion, and the DHARMa zero-inflation test will determine whether a zero-inflated negative binomial is warranted.

From that we can see that the negative binomial model out performs the Poisson model, and in the negative binomial model there is no extra zero-inflation and it isn’t really improved with a non-linearity.

Write-up prompt

From that it looks like the linear negative binomial model is appropriate. It is better than Poisson, the gam had an edf of 1.1 and the zero-inflation test had a p-value of 0.8057. Can you write a quarto document for this analysis that includes a methods section, results section and references?

Since you’ve already established that (1) the negative binomial model fits substantially better than the Poisson, (2) there is no evidence of nonlinearity (GAM edf ≈ 1.1), and (3) there is no evidence of excess zeros (DHARMa zero-inflation test p = 0.806), a simple negative binomial GLM is the most parsimonious model for inference on the relationship between soil crust cover and recruit abundance in df_rec_saw.

Below is a complete Quarto document template.

The quarto document that Copilot produced didn’t include any references, even though I explicitly asked for them.

One thing I would recommend is replacing the generic Results text with automatically generated values such as the coefficient estimate, standard error, confidence interval, AIC difference, and p-value from the crust effect. That makes the report fully reproducible and publication-ready.

Update to write-up prompt

You didn’t include any references. Can you please update the quarto file by adding appropriate references and the bibtex file that would go with them and add the automatically generated values like you suggested.

Good point. The previous version cited packages in the text but did not actually use citation keys, so nothing would appear in the References section.

A better approach is to cite the statistical methods that justify:

  1. Generalized linear models.
  2. Negative binomial regression for overdispersed counts.
  3. Generalized additive models.
  4. DHARMa residual diagnostics.
  5. R itself.

Below is an updated Quarto document that:

  • automatically inserts coefficient estimates, standard errors, p-values, and incidence rate ratios;
  • reports the zero-inflation test p-value;
  • reports the GAM edf;
  • generates publication-style results text automatically;
  • includes proper scholarly citations;
  • produces a populated References section.

One additional improvement I would make for a report intended for publication would be to report the actual predicted effect over a biologically meaningful range (e.g. 0% to 50% crust cover) rather than the default “one-unit increase” on a 0-1 scale. That is generally much easier for readers to interpret.

Let’s see the effect of the Copilot suggestion.

Okay, update the report as you suggested to the actual predicted effect over the range 0% ot 50%.

Yes, I think that’s a much more meaningful effect size. A “1-unit increase” corresponds to going from 0% crust to 100% crust cover, which is not especially intuitive. Reporting the predicted change from 0% to 50% crust cover is easier for readers to interpret.

Replace the “Effect of soil crust cover” section with the following.

You could also strengthen the interpretation further by reporting a contrast across the observed interquartile range of crust cover rather than an arbitrary 0% to 50% change:

q <- quantile(df$crust, probs = c(0.25, 0.75))

effect_iqr <- exp(beta * diff(q))

and then write:

“Plots at the 75th percentile of soil crust cover were predicted to have X times the recruitment of plots at the 25th percentile.”

This is often preferred in ecological journals because it describes the effect over a realistic range actually observed in the data rather than a hypothetical range.

I am not sure how many more suggestions it will make, but let’s leave it there.
